covalent.note: Covalent radius; PubChem's values are those of Cordero et al., Dalton Trans. 2008, 2832.

vdw.note: Van der Waals radius (Los Alamos National Laboratory).

electronAffinity.note: PubChem lists no electron affinity for this element.

allen.note: Configuration energy (Allen electronegativity) in eV, not converted to the Pauling-like scale; Mann 2000a.

crust.note: Jefferson Lab estimate for Earth's crust, via PubChem ('1.9×10¹ milligrams per kilogram').

ocean.note: Jefferson Lab estimate for sea water, via PubChem ('5×10⁻¹ milligrams per liter').

solar.note: Proto-solar (4.567 Ga ago) elemental mass fraction, column 'Elemental Mass Fractions' of ESM Table A13; the table gives no uncertainty (relative sigma of N(E) in Table 6 applies).

solarLogEps.note: A(E) = log10(N_E/N_H) + 12, 'Solar System Present' log (E/H)+12; basis: solar (photospheric) value; unc = 1 sigma in dex as printed.

body.note: In a 70 kg reference adult (ICRP Publication 23, 1975, Table 110).

crystal.reference: Wyckoff, R. W. G. (1963). Crystal Structures 1, 7.
crystal.note: Low-temperature solid only, at 4.2 K, value from Wyckoff's compilation (no primary reference in CIF). Schuch & Mills 1970 (COD 9012480, DOI 10.1063/1.1672899) report space group P213 at 20 K, but that COD entry lists only 4 N atoms per cell (half of the 8 atoms of the 4 N2 molecules), so it was not used.

production.basis: plant production of ammonia, nitrogen content

tonnesPerYear.note: World plant production of ammonia, nitrogen content, 2025 (USGS: 160,000 thousand metric tons).

unitValue.note: Price, average, free on board Gulf Coast, dollars per short ton [Nitrogen (Fixed)—Ammonia], 2025; per kg of the material named, as USGS gives it.

origin.note: Read off Fig. 39 at the dotted 'age of the Sun' line (t = 9.2 Gyr after the Big Bang, 4.6 Gyr ago): pixel fractions of the stacked areas (agb 0.741, massive_stars 0.259); quantised to 0.05. Stack height 72 px. Cross-check with the paper's text: '74% of N are produced by AGB stars' (figure reading 0.741).

plantRole.text: Taken up as nitrate or ammonium; part of amino acids, proteins, nucleic acids and chlorophyll, and the nutrient that most often limits plant growth.

humanRole.text: Part of every amino acid, protein and nucleic acid; obtained from dietary protein.

history.nameOrigin: From the French nitrogène, built from the Greek nitron ('native soda', i.e. nitre) and -genes ('producing'), because it is a constituent of nitre.
history.note: Scheele, Cavendish and Priestley were studying the same unbreathable residue of air at about the same time.

prose.text: Nitrogen is a colourless, unreactive gas that makes up most of the air we breathe, yet it is also a building block of every protein and every strand of DNA. Plants cannot use the gas directly, because the triple bond holding the two atoms of N₂ together is extraordinarily strong; legumes such as peas and clover solve this by housing bacteria in root nodules that turn it into ammonia. A nitrogen atom, [He] 2s² 2p³, has three 2p electrons, one in each p orbital with parallel spins (ground term ⁴S°₃/₂). This half-filled subshell is so stable that nitrogen's first ionisation energy, 1402 kJ/mol, exceeds oxygen's 1314 kJ/mol.
